considerations.detail: Miriam, Amaka, Joke, Princess, Titi, and Grace each dramatize rejection or distance, which reinforces the theme but also creates a similar beat pattern across multiple scenes. The version of the script where one or two of those relationships carry more distinct emotional functions would sharpen the feature’s variety and keep each encounter feeling newly charged.

considerations.area: The location footprint is broad for a drama.
considerations.detail: Hospitals, churches, schools, homes, campuses, villages, cafes, and streets across multiple time periods create a sizable production map. A simplification pass that folds some of the conversation scenes into fewer recurring spaces would protect the story while making the shoot more efficient.

considerations.area: The lead spans multiple ages.
considerations.detail: Ben appears as an infant, child, teen, and adult, which means the package needs careful age casting and continuity planning around the facial condition. That is manageable, but the cleanest version of the production will keep the number of distinct Ben ages as lean as the story allows.

considerations.area: The script sits in a modest-budget prestige lane.
considerations.detail: This is not a spectacle piece; its value is in performance, specificity, and emotional identification. Positioning it as a festival-to-streaming drama with a strong lead and a culturally rooted hook will serve it better than trying to broaden it into a larger commercial package.

buyer_appeal.lane: Festival-to-platform drama / faith-adjacent prestige indie
buyer_appeal.detail: The project can be anchored by one strong lead performance rather than a name-heavy ensemble, which makes it viable for a director-driven package. Its Nigerian specificity, church-adjacent moral debate, and underdog authorship arc give it a clear diaspora and streamer acquisition lane.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to turn autobiography into a prestige human drama.
director_appeal.detail: The film gives a director a chance to shape a life story into a coherent emotional arc while working with a contained dramatic vocabulary: homes, schools, churches, hospitals, and campuses. It will attract directors who like actor-led material, culturally specific realism, and the challenge of making a testimonial voice feel cinematic.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with festival-drama instincts, or established indie filmmakers who already work in performance-forward, socially rooted storytelling. This material rewards restraint, period texture, and an ability to stage memory, testimony, and emotional humiliation without over-stylizing them.

lead_characters.hook: Ben is an observant, wounded, self-mythologizing young man who grows up carrying a visible facial difference, a bruised family history, and a stubborn belief that his life can still mean something. He is bookish, lonely, morally argumentative, and deeply verbal — the kind of protagonist who turns pain into philosophy because philosophy is how he survives it.
lead_characters.name: BEN
lead_characters.demographics: Male · 3 months to 30s · Nigerian · facial deformity / visible medical condition
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Eddie Redmayne in The Theory of Everything and Riz Ahmed in Sound of Metal — a role where the body itself becomes part of the emotional language, and the actor has to carry intelligence, humiliation, longing, and resolve at once. Dramatic leads who want a transformation role with awards-adjacent emotional range will chase this, especially performers looking for a part that can move from childhood vulnerability to adult authorship.

lead_characters.hook: Ben’s mother is practical, overburdened, and emotionally blunt, a woman who keeps the household moving while carrying her own disappointments and resentments. She is not written as sentimental comfort; she is the force of survival, discipline, and hard reality in the home.
lead_characters.name: MOTHER
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of maternal role that gave Viola Davis in Fences and Octavia Spencer in The Help a chance to play authority, fatigue, and love in the same breath. Character actresses who want a grounded, scene-stealing family anchor will see a part with moral weight and strong dramatic presence.

lead_characters.hook: Ben’s father is a damaged, inconsistent presence marked by drinking, smoking, absence, and a history that includes war, work, and disappointment. He is less a stable parent than a symbol of broken inheritance, the man whose failures help define the son’s self-making.
lead_characters.name: FATHER
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted father role that gave Bryan Cranston in The Judge and Jeffrey Wright in Fences room to play regret, authority, and emotional distance. Veteran dramatic actors who specialize in morally compromised patriarchs will be drawn to the chance to make absence feel active.

lead_characters.hook: Miriam is one of Ben’s early romantic possibilities, but she is also a social mirror: warm enough to invite hope, guarded enough to refuse it. She reads as a young woman aware of social pressure and unwilling to become someone else’s rescue fantasy.
lead_characters.name: MIRIAM
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Aunjanue Ellis in King Richard and Danielle Brooks in The Color Purple a chance to combine warmth, self-possession, and emotional boundary-setting. Actors who want a brief but memorable part with real dignity and chemistry will respond to it.

lead_characters.hook: Quadri is a schoolmate who briefly gives Ben companionship and the feeling of being seen. He functions as a small but important human bridge in a story otherwise dominated by exclusion and departure.
lead_characters.name: QUADRI
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting youth role that gives a young actor the naturalism space of Moonlight’s teenage ensemble or The Florida Project’s kid friendships — small scenes that carry emotional truth. Emerging teen actors and casting directors looking for authenticity in school-age roles will notice it.

lead_characters.hook: Emeka is another school connection for Ben, a bright, temporary ally whose departure reinforces the film’s pattern of impermanence. He helps define Ben’s loneliness by being one more person life does not let him keep.
lead_characters.name: EMEKA
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor the understated, lived-in texture of a supporting turn in Boyhood or The Last Black Man in San Francisco. It’s a clean, human part for a performer who can make a few scenes feel like a real friendship.

lead_characters.hook: Shade is sharp, skeptical, and emotionally armored, with a worldview shaped by family hurt rather than sentiment. She gives the film one of its clearest arguments about forgiveness versus retaliation, and she says it without softening the edges.
lead_characters.name: SHADE
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-part that gave Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Teyonah Parris in If Beale Street Could Talk room to play intelligence with bite. Actors who like dialogue-forward roles with attitude and conviction will be drawn to her.

lead_characters.hook: Tim is a friend carrying his own father wound, and his cynicism gives the film a counterpoint to Ben’s moral searching. He is the voice of hard-earned bitterness, the person who makes forgiveness sound naïve and survival sound transactional.
lead_characters.name: TIM
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the emotionally guarded, lived-in work seen in The Bear’s more wounded supporting turns or in Manchester by the Sea’s family confrontations. It’s attractive to actors who can make restraint feel loaded.

lead_characters.hook: Prince is a friend and commentator who helps externalize the social pressure around dating, status, and ambition. He is part chorus, part peer, and part reality check.
lead_characters.name: PRINCE
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting friend role that gives a performer the easy, natural rhythm of a coming-of-age ensemble piece like Dope or Superbad. It’s a useful part for a young actor who can play banter and social observation without overreaching.

lead_characters.hook: Amaka is desired, guarded, and socially protected, with a presence that turns Ben’s longing into embarrassment and class tension. She is less a love interest than a gatekeeper to a world Ben wants but cannot enter cleanly.
lead_characters.name: AMAKA
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the cool, socially legible authority of a character in a teen drama like The Half of It or Never Have I Ever. It’s a compact part with strong attitude and a memorable rejection beat.

lead_characters.hook: Joke is flirtation, possibility, and humiliation all at once — a woman who initially seems open, then reveals the social and physical barriers Ben cannot talk his way through. She gives the film one of its clearest emotional reversals.
lead_characters.name: JOKE
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late teens to 20s · ebony, petite
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the sharp, painful turn of a relationship scene in Blue Valentine or The Spectacular Now. It’s a strong fit for performers who can pivot from warmth to rejection in a single exchange.

lead_characters.hook: Princess is brisk, dismissive, and socially unavailable, another woman whose response teaches Ben that desire is not enough. She is a clean embodiment of the film’s repeated lesson that attraction alone does not overcome stigma or status.
lead_characters.name: PRINCESS
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but memorable role that gives an actress a sharp rejection scene with immediate audience recognition. It suits performers who can make a few lines land with social authority.

lead_characters.hook: Titi is rumored, desired, and socially complicated, which makes her feel both alluring and dangerous in the eyes of the campus. She adds another layer to Ben’s romantic education: attraction is never separate from gossip, reputation, and public judgment.
lead_characters.name: TITI
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late teens to 20s · ebony, petite
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of part that gives an actress the textured ambiguity seen in campus dramas and social melodramas. It’s attractive to performers who can play charm under scrutiny.

lead_characters.hook: Grace is reserved, principled, and institutionally protected by faith rules that shape her relationship with Ben. She is not just a love interest; she is the point where desire collides with doctrine and social order.
lead_characters.name: GRACE
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the moral gravity of a faith-based drama lead in miniature, similar to the grounded restraint seen in The Chosen or The Leftovers’ more devout characters. It’s a strong fit for performers who can play conviction without flattening into piety.

lead_characters.hook: Antonia is blunt enough to say what others only imply: Ben’s face has shaped his romantic life. She functions as an unsparing friend, a truth-teller who gives the story one of its most direct social verdicts.
lead_characters.name: ANTONIA
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actress deliver the hard-edged honesty of a supporting turn in Insecure or Shrinking. It’s a compact part with a memorable line and a clear point of view.

lead_characters.hook: The Foreigner is a listening device for Ben’s self-explanation, a neutral ear that lets the script turn autobiography into argument. The character exists to receive Ben’s worldview and make it legible to an outside audience.
lead_characters.name: FOREIGNER
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a performer the conversational function of an interviewer or framing device, similar to the listener roles in documentary-style dramas. It suits actors comfortable with reactive, grounded scene work.

lead_characters.hook: The Author is a peer witness to Ben’s self-construction, someone who validates his persistence and helps turn the final stretch into a statement of arrival. The role is less about plot than about recognition.
lead_characters.name: AUTHOR
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor the reflective, affirming energy of a mentor or peer in a literary drama. It’s a clean fit for performers who can make encouragement feel earned.

lead_characters.hook: Pastor Thomas is charismatic in public and morally compromised in private, which makes him one of the story’s clearest embodiments of hypocrisy. He is the kind of authority figure whose collapse forces Ben to rethink forgiveness as a lived principle rather than a slogan.
lead_characters.name: PASTOR THOMAS
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the layered authority of a prestige-TV pastor or community leader, with the moral contradiction space seen in The Righteous Gemstones or Greenleaf. Veteran character actors who enjoy playing public virtue and private collapse will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: The Pastor’s Wife is a domestic casualty inside a public moral system, and her presence gives the church storyline its emotional cost. She is a silent witness to the gap between doctrine and behavior.
lead_characters.name: PASTOR’S WIFE
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actress the compressed pain of a scene in a church drama or domestic thriller. It suits performers who can communicate distress and endurance with minimal dialogue.

lead_characters.hook: The Diviner gives Ben a mystical explanation for his suffering, adding a spiritual register to the film’s worldview. The character helps widen the story beyond realism into belief, omen, and fate.
lead_characters.name: DIVINER
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the enigmatic authority of a seer or oracle in a mythic drama. It’s ideal for performers who can make a few lines feel ceremonial and consequential.

lead_characters.hook: The Talkmate is a conversational witness who helps Ben articulate the meaning of his suffering and the logic of his distance from family. The role functions as a philosophical sounding board rather than a plot driver.
lead_characters.name: TALKMATE
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the intimate, dialogue-based space of a confessional drama or interview scene. It suits performers who can listen well and land reflective material.

lead_characters.hook: The Motorist is a brief but humanizing presence in the accident sequence, a stranger who checks on Ben after the van hit. The character reinforces the film’s recurring theme that care often comes from outside the family.
lead_characters.name: MOTORIST
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small role that gives an actor a single scene of immediate empathy, similar to the memorable one-scene helpers in indie dramas. It’s a clean, grounded part.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is serious and investigative, but it has a strong human pulse: newsroom banter, Don’s domestic warmth, Adamson’s banal sleaze, and the moral outrage of the press-club scenes. It reads as a prestige historical thriller with a newsroom conscience.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A murdered reporter story is familiar territory, but this one lands with a specific historical charge: local corruption, organized crime, newsroom politics, and the birth of a national investigative community. The result feels both recognizable and freshly situated in a very particular American moment.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The pilot establishes its engine early with Don Bolles’ bombing, then quickly turns into a pursuit of Adamson, Emprise, and the larger political web. The opening, the attack, and the newsroom scramble make the premise easy to explain in two sentences.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Phoenix in 1976 feels lived-in through the Statehouse, the Ivanhoe, the country club, the hotel corridors, and the newsroom ecosystem. The script also builds a wider civic world — police, politicians, publishers, reporters, and old-money networks — that can keep generating story.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediate and legible: a journalist is bombed, the newsroom mobilizes, and the case widens into corruption at the top. The period setting narrows the audience a bit, but the true-story engine and newsroom-investigation frame give it real buyer-facing momentum.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The pilot keeps turning the screw: bombing, source trail, Adamson’s surrender, the arrest, the release, the deeper suspicion, and then the final threat to Winters. Each reveal opens a new door rather than closing the case, which is exactly what a series pilot needs.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The pilot is built on a murder investigation, but it keeps hinting at deeper systems: political protection, institutional cowardice, and the cost of telling the truth in public. The final beat with Winters’ car on fire suggests the conspiracy is not just historical background but an expanding threat.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script leans into a less-familiar corner of American history and makes the journalism world feel active rather than decorative. The choice to split the story between Phoenix and Indianapolis, and to center a Black woman editor in a white male press culture, gives it a sharper identity than a standard true-crime procedural.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Don, Winters, Myrta, and Garcia each bring a distinct angle on the story, and the pilot gives them clear emotional stakes around truth, fear, and professional duty. The series potential is strongest in Winters and Garcia as ongoing investigators, while Myrta adds a compelling parallel newsroom track.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Winters/Don, Winters/Early, Garcia/Dryden, Myrta/Nina, and the press-club network all create usable recurring dynamics. The show still orbits a few central figures, but the supporting relationships are active enough to sustain a multi-threaded series.

whats_special.headline: THE ARIZONA PROJECT has the bones of a prestige limited series with real staying power: a true-crime newsroom thriller anchored by a memorable investigative lead, a socially rich 1970s Southwest setting, and a conspiracy that keeps widening after the bomb goes off. It’s the kind of material that can attract strong actors because every major role plays a different facet of truth-telling under pressure.

strengths.evidence: Don Bolles’ bombing, the newsroom scramble, and the widening trail through Adamson, Emprise, and Arizona power brokers.
strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of true-story foundation that gives a buyer both urgency and legitimacy: a murder, a newsroom, and a conspiracy that can expand across a limited series. Prestige buyers and awards-minded streamers are the natural home because the material already carries cultural weight and episode-to-episode propulsion.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The pilot has a built-in historical engine.

strengths.evidence: His newsroom argument with Early, his desk-digging through Don’s files, and his decision to keep pushing after the arrest.
strengths.what_it_means: John Winters is the audience’s entry point into the case, and his mix of intellect, insecurity, and moral stubbornness can carry multiple episodes without flattening out. Actors who specialize in smart, watchful, slightly haunted leads will see a role with long-run prestige value.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Winters gives the series a durable POV.

strengths.evidence: Her call for the IRE conference to go to Phoenix and her speech about speaking for Don.
strengths.what_it_means: Her Indianapolis track turns the story from a local murder into a national press movement, which gives the series scale beyond one city and one investigation. That opens the door to a broader audience of viewers who respond to newsroom ensemble drama and to actors looking for a commanding, high-status editorial role.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Myrta Pulliam broadens the show’s reach.

strengths.evidence: The Goldwater/Rosenzweig history, the Ivanhoe, the country club, the statehouse, and the newsroom bullpen.
strengths.what_it_means: The script isn’t just using 1976 as wallpaper; it builds a civic ecosystem of old families, country clubs, bars, statehouse corridors, and newsroom hierarchies that can keep generating story. That kind of textured world is attractive to premium buyers because it supports both case-of-the-week movement and long-form institutional drama.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The Phoenix world feels socially specific.

strengths.evidence: Garcia’s interrogation of Adamson, his suspicion of Chief Lozier, and his private meeting with Babbitt.
strengths.what_it_means: The police side of the story gives the series a parallel engine that can run alongside the journalism track, which is valuable for pacing and episode structure. A grounded, procedural-minded actor will be drawn to the role because it plays competence, suspicion, and institutional pressure in the same frame.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Garcia adds a second investigative lane.

strengths.evidence: Rosalie at the hospital, the children arriving, and the newsroom reacting to Don’s death.
strengths.what_it_means: The script keeps the investigation human by tying it to Don’s family, Rosalie’s grief, and the newsroom’s fear, which makes the procedural material land harder. That balance is attractive to buyers because it widens the audience beyond pure true-crime fans into character-driven prestige drama viewers.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The pilot understands emotional stakes inside procedure.

classification.tone: grounded, tense, procedural, morally urgent

considerations.area: The pilot carries a lot of historical names.
considerations.detail: The script is rich in real people, public institutions, and named brands, which is great for specificity but means the clearance path should be mapped early. A next pass could also decide which historical references are essential to the pilot’s immediate propulsion and which can stay in the series bible, protecting the same texture with fewer on-page dependencies.

considerations.area: The opening hour covers a lot of ground.
considerations.detail: The pilot moves from Don’s home life to the newsroom, the bombing, the police investigation, the Indianapolis press world, and multiple flashbacks. One lever would be to keep the emotional spine even tighter around Winters and Myrta so the audience always knows which thread is carrying them through the historical sprawl.

considerations.area: The investigation can sharpen around one central question.
considerations.detail: The script already asks the right questions about Adamson, Emprise, and who benefits from the hit, and the final car-fire beat proves the conspiracy is still alive. A next pass could foreground one dominant mystery per act so each turn lands with even more force before the larger web opens up.

considerations.area: The period footprint is manageable but specific.
considerations.detail: This is a grounded 1976 series with newsroom, hotel, police, hospital, statehouse, bar, and apartment work rather than large-scale spectacle. The version of the show that keeps Phoenix streets, newsroom interiors, and a few signature locations recurring would protect the period feel while keeping the production footprint disciplined.

considerations.area: The child and family material adds emotional weight.
considerations.detail: Don’s seven kids and Diane’s sign-language scenes give the story a strong domestic counterpoint, and that family presence helps the tragedy land. If the series wants to stay lean, the family can remain emotionally vivid while the day-to-day logistics stay concentrated in a smaller number of recurring home scenes.

lead_characters.hook: A sharp, bookish Arizona Republic reporter who wants to be taken seriously and keeps finding himself in the room when history turns ugly. He’s intellectually restless, professionally hungry, and just self-aware enough to know he’s being pulled into something bigger than his own ambition.
lead_characters.name: John Winters
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Matthew Rhys in The Americans — a cerebral, watchful lead whose intelligence is inseparable from anxiety and moral pressure. It gives an actor the chance to play investigative rigor, grief, and escalating paranoia while carrying the audience through a conspiracy that keeps widening.

lead_characters.hook: A polished, formidable Indianapolis editor who moves easily in elite rooms but never loses her edge or her sense of what journalism is for. She carries authority without performing it, and the script makes her both socially fluent and emotionally exacting.
lead_characters.name: Myrta Pulliam
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kerry Washington in Scandal — a woman who can command a room, weaponize composure, and let private feeling leak through the armor at just the right moment. It gives an actor a prestige editorial role with public force, private ache, and a national-scale moral mission.

lead_characters.hook: A Phoenix detective with deep local roots, a working cop’s instincts, and a growing sense that the official story is too neat to be true. He’s disciplined, skeptical, and quietly troubled by the possibility that the people around him are protecting more than the public.
lead_characters.name: Francisco (Frank) Garcia
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Peña in End of Watch — a grounded lawman role that mixes procedural competence with personal pressure and moral alertness. It gives an actor a steady, watchable center while still letting suspicion and conscience do the dramatic work.

lead_characters.hook: A warm, funny, relentless investigative reporter whose charm makes him disarming and whose curiosity makes him dangerous to the people he writes about. He’s a family man with a reporter’s appetite for trouble, and the script frames him as both beloved colleague and living warning sign.
lead_characters.name: Don Bolles
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Trumbo — a charismatic, complicated public figure whose wit and humanity make the danger around him feel even sharper. It gives an actor a role with warmth, authority, and tragic inevitability, the kind of part that can anchor a prestige campaign even in limited screen time.

lead_characters.hook: Don’s wife and the emotional ballast of the Bolles home, she reads as practical, loving, and already used to living beside a man whose work keeps pulling him away. Her hospital scenes give the story its domestic truth and its most devastating human scale.
lead_characters.name: Rosalie Bolles
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Laura Linney in The Savages — a woman whose love is expressed through restraint, competence, and the ability to absorb pain without turning it into speech. It gives an actor a deeply felt family role that can break the audience open in a handful of scenes.

lead_characters.hook: The Arizona Republic’s editor-in-chief, carrying the authority of a newsroom boss who knows when to push and when to shut a conversation down. He’s pragmatic, protective, and increasingly aware that the paper is standing on dangerous ground.
lead_characters.name: Bob Early
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of J.K. Simmons in Spotlight — a newsroom authority figure who can turn a single line into institutional pressure. It gives an actor the chance to play command, grief, and editorial judgment without ever leaving the room.

lead_characters.hook: A statehouse editor with a dry wit and a reporter’s instinct for how power actually works. He functions as one of the newsroom’s practical brains, but the script gives him enough texture to feel like a real working journalist rather than a utility player.
lead_characters.name: Bernie Wynn
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor — a quiet, observant professional role where intelligence and weariness live in the same frame. It gives an actor a strong supporting part built on authority, skepticism, and lived-in newsroom rhythm.

lead_characters.hook: Garcia’s partner, a hard-edged detective who brings blunt force and streetwise confidence to the investigation. He’s the kind of cop who can crack a joke, read a room, and still make the case feel dangerous.
lead_characters.name: Dan Dryden
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire — a rough, vivid supporting cop role that can steal scenes through attitude and timing. It gives an actor a meaty law-enforcement part with texture, humor, and menace.

lead_characters.hook: A bulky, smug, low-rent operator who moves through the world with the confidence of a man who has learned that stupidity can be a shield. He’s not glamorous evil; he’s banal, opportunistic, and infuriatingly comfortable in his own skin.
lead_characters.name: John Harvey Adamson
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Walter Hauser in Black Bird — a grotesque, oddly magnetic criminal role where the performance lives in behavior, not speeches. It gives an actor the chance to make a contemptible man unforgettable through physicality, timing, and dead-eyed self-regard.

lead_characters.hook: The publisher and family matriarch who carries institutional power with polished restraint. She’s elegant, controlled, and quietly aware of the distance between family loyalty and editorial responsibility.
lead_characters.name: Nina Pulliam
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Meryl Streep in The Post — a woman whose authority is expressed through stillness, precision, and the weight of a legacy institution. It gives an actor a high-status supporting role that can define the room with very little movement.

considerations.detail: The final stretch works because Eddie stops apologizing for himself and starts leading, especially once he uses the tail, the limo-company log, and the fake-star persona to draw Robert out. The version of the script where that shift is slightly more foregrounded in the earlier search beats would make the payoff feel even bigger.

considerations.area: The warehouse climax is production-friendly but busy.
considerations.detail: The final battle is mostly practical and contained, which keeps it in a manageable feature lane, but it does ask for a lot of bodies, weapons, and stunt choreography in one space. If needed, the version of the climax where a few of the weapon gags are consolidated would protect the chaos while making the shoot cleaner.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streaming comedy-thriller / premium cable satire lane
buyer_appeal.detail: The script can be packaged around three strong leads and a director with ensemble-comedy chops, rather than requiring a tentpole-level effects or action package. The celebrity-satire angle, Black Hollywood setting, and social-media fame engine give it a clear marketing hook for streamers looking for a contemporary, conversation-friendly original.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a celebrity satire that still plays like a propulsive kidnapping thriller.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to orchestrate a big comic ensemble across airport, red carpet, casting office, and warehouse set pieces without needing heavy VFX. It will appeal to filmmakers who know how to make dialogue scenes feel kinetic and who can turn a contained contemporary world into a highly legible commercial ride.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Second-feature or established indie-comedy directors with a strong ensemble reel, especially those who like social satire, pop-culture specificity, and performance-forward staging. This material rewards directors who can keep the jokes sharp while still landing the tension of a rescue movie and the emotional turn underneath the absurdity.

lead_characters.hook: Tosin is a loud, self-mythologizing actor who lives on validation, posts like he’s already a legend, and treats every encounter like a step toward greater fame. Under the swagger, though, he’s deeply insecure, hungry to be seen, and more vulnerable than he admits, which makes him both funny and sympathetic even when he’s unbearable.
lead_characters.name: Tosin Morohunfola
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Donald Glover in Atlanta when the character’s self-image is the joke and the wound at the same time — a role that lets an actor play vanity, panic, and sudden humility in one arc. Actors who can do fast comic rhythm but still land emotional self-recognition will chase it, especially performers looking for a lead that can carry a movie and still feel human.

lead_characters.hook: Eddie is the overlooked best friend who has spent so long orbiting someone else’s spotlight that he’s almost invisible to the world and to himself. He’s funny, anxious, loyal, and desperate to matter, and the script lets him evolve from a guy begging for a break into the one person with enough heart and hustle to actually save the day.
lead_characters.name: Eddie Jones
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the breakout-comic-to-hero lane of Lakeith Stanfield in Sorry to Bother You or Donald Faison in a prestige ensemble — a role where awkwardness becomes authority by the end. Actors who want a star-making underdog part with real emotional lift will chase it, because the arc gives them both broad comedy and a genuine leadership turn.

lead_characters.hook: Kelly is the grounded counterweight to all the ego in the movie: observant, emotionally guarded, and carrying grief that makes her wary of easy intimacy. She’s the kind of character who sees through performance immediately, but she’s also open enough to be moved by sincerity, which gives her a quiet but powerful presence.
lead_characters.name: Kelly
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the grounded emotional anchor territory of Jurnee Smollett in Lovecraft Country or Regina Hall in Support the Girls — a role that lets an actress play restraint, intelligence, and late-breaking vulnerability. Actresses looking for a part that can hold the movie’s heart without becoming sentimental will want this.

lead_characters.hook: Robert is a bitter former actor who has turned his own resentment into a hostage business, and he carries himself like a man who believes the world stole his rightful close-up. He’s theatrical, wounded, and delusional in a way that makes him both funny and dangerous, especially once his old superhero identity is revealed.
lead_characters.name: Robert Pupkin
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the unhinged-villain showcase territory of Michael Keaton in Birdman or Willem Dafoe in The Lighthouse — a role where grievance, performance, and menace all feed each other. Character actors who love playing intelligence curdled into obsession will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Masha is Robert’s feral enforcer, a weapon-obsessed chaos agent who can pivot from groveling to lethal in a beat. She’s not just muscle; she’s a comic menace with a strange devotion to Robert that makes her unpredictable and scene-stealing.
lead_characters.name: Masha Bernhard
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the feral-sidekick lane of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Jennifer Jason Leigh in The Hateful Eight — a role that lets an actor play volatility, physicality, and dark comic timing. Performers who want a memorable supporting turn with action and attitude will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Credenza is Tosin’s ex and a walking contradiction: calm one minute, volcanic the next, then suddenly spiritually centered and still carrying a blade of resentment. She’s funny because she’s so specific, but she also gives the movie a real emotional history with Tosin that deepens the stakes around his selfishness.
lead_characters.name: Credenza
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the ex-with-volatility showcase territory of Tessa Thompson in Sorry to Bother You or Taraji P. Henson in Empire — a role that lets an actress swing between rage, humor, and wounded intimacy. Actors who like a part with bite, history, and a late-stage redemption turn will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Julian is one half of the Gangstas, a streetwise skeptic who keeps getting pulled into absurd celebrity-adjacent chaos while trying to maintain some dignity. He’s funny because he’s always half-convinced this is a scam, and that skepticism gives him a grounded edge inside the madness.
lead_characters.name: Julian
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sharp-supporting-comic lane of Method Man in The Deuce or Donald Faison in a buddy ensemble — a role that rewards timing, reaction, and chemistry. Actors who like to steal scenes without carrying the whole movie will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Namir is Julian’s louder counterpart, more suspicious, more impulsive, and often the first to escalate a situation into chaos. He’s a comic pressure valve with real presence, and the script uses him as both threat and punchline.
lead_characters.name: Namir
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the high-energy sidekick territory of Omar Benson Miller in Ballers or Ice Cube in a broad ensemble — a role that gives an actor swagger, reaction comedy, and physical business. Performers who can dominate a scene with attitude will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Karen is one of the Groupies, but she’s not just a joke; she’s a hyper-committed celebrity obsessive who treats access like religion. Her earnestness makes her funny, and her willingness to go along with the madness gives the ensemble a useful comic engine.
lead_characters.name: Karen
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the broad-comic-ensemble lane of a character like the women in Girls Trip or a sharp supporting player in a Tina Fey comedy — a role that lives on timing and commitment. Actors who enjoy playing heightened obsession with sincerity will have fun with it.

lead_characters.hook: Sharon is the most openly chaotic of the Groupies, the one who can turn a celebrity sighting into a full-body event. She’s a comic wild card, but the script also lets her register as part of a real fan ecosystem rather than a throwaway gag.
lead_characters.name: Sharon
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the scene-stealing supporting-comedy lane of a performer like Natasha Rothwell in Insecure — a part that rewards big reactions and precise timing. Actors who like to make a small role memorable will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: McClaren is the Groupies’ most theatrical member, the one who can pivot from fan to guide to underground celebrity broker without blinking. She has the most overtly absurd comic voice in the trio, which makes her feel like a secret weapon whenever she appears.
lead_characters.name: McClaren
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the offbeat-comic-supporting lane of a role like Aidy Bryant in a sketchy ensemble or Quinta Brunson in early breakout work — a part that rewards specificity and fearless commitment. Actors who want a memorable comic signature will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Rishab is one of Tosin’s agents, all industry polish on the surface and total indifference underneath. He’s useful because he embodies the machine that keeps people like Tosin chasing approval while never quite delivering it.
lead_characters.name: Rishab
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the dry-industry-supporting lane of a role like the agents and managers in Entourage or The Studio — a part that plays status, dismissal, and comic deadpan. Character actors who can make bureaucracy funny will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Jessalyn is Tosin’s manager, and she’s all breezy professional cheer until the moment she reveals how transactional the business really is. She gives the movie a sharp industry voice and helps turn the celebrity satire into something more pointed.
lead_characters.name: Jessalyn
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sharp-manager lane of a role like the agents in The Devil Wears Prada or the Hollywood operators in Entourage — a part that lets an actor play charm and calculation at once. Performers who can make business talk feel like comedy will want it.

lead_characters.hook: Ibrahim is the casting director who treats actors like raw material and the room like his personal kingdom. He’s smug, predatory, and absurdly self-important, which makes him a perfect embodiment of the industry’s gatekeeping side.
lead_characters.name: Ibrahim Saltzman
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the power-broker supporting lane of a role like the casting-office figures in The Player or Barry — a part that lets an actor play authority, vanity, and passive cruelty. Character actors who enjoy playing the gatekeeper will chase it.

lead_characters.hook: Lauren is the TMZ-style reporter who knows how to turn chaos into content and content into leverage. She’s fast, sharp, and opportunistic, but she also functions as a narrative bridge between the celebrity world and the real-world search for Tosin.
lead_characters.name: Lauren Rolaché
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the fast-talking media-lane of a role like a sharp correspondent in a newsroom comedy or a gossip reporter in a prestige satire — a part that rewards speed and authority. Actors who can make exposition feel like entertainment will want it.

lead_characters.hook: The VIP Man is a mythic access broker who treats celebrity entry like a sacred craft and speaks as if he’s guarding a hidden kingdom. He’s ridiculous and oddly noble at the same time, which makes him one of the script’s most memorable comic inventions.
lead_characters.name: The VIP Man
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the larger-than-life comic-supporting lane of a role like a Coen brothers oddball or a prestige-comedy eccentric — a part that lets an actor build a whole mythology in a few scenes. Character actors who love a singular, quotable creation will chase it.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is very identifiable: raunchy, talky, self-mocking, and built around men and women who are both horny and emotionally bruised. The script knows exactly how far it wants to push the banter, and the repeated sexual wordplay gives it a consistent comic signature.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of middle-aged dating chaos is instantly understandable, and the script finds a fresh lane by making golf, strip clubs, office crushes, and ex-spouses all part of the same social ecosystem. What makes it memorable is the accumulation of awkward encounters rather than one singular, high-concept twist.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands quickly: Kevin is newly divorced, bad at dating, and keeps getting blindsided by women who are more complicated than he expects. The bar, office, golf, and wedding beats all reinforce the same engine, so the premise stays legible even as the romantic entanglements multiply.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Florida singles world has texture: bars, golf courses, office cubes, strip clubs, and restaurant culture all feel like part of one adult mating ground. The setting is more of a social container than a rule-based world, but it does generate repeated comic situations and a clear lifestyle vibe.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and the dating-war setup has a clear audience, especially for adult viewers who like relationship comedies with frank sexual banter. Its appeal is narrower than a four-quadrant rom-com because the humor is heavily adult and the voice is very specific to this group of middle-aged singles.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps moving through a steady chain of dates, bar scenes, golf outings, and romantic reversals, so it rarely sits still for long. The momentum is driven more by episodic comic set-pieces than by a single escalating external goal, which keeps it lively but not especially propulsive.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the jokes, the script keeps returning to loneliness, fear of aging alone, and the desire to be chosen for something deeper than sex. That emotional layer is present enough to give the comedy a heart, though the script mostly keeps it in dialogue rather than letting it accumulate through quieter turns.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a very specific adult-dating lane and leans hard into sexual embarrassment, which gives it a recognizable comic identity. At the same time, the underlying structure is familiar romantic-comedy territory: divorce, rebound dating, mistaken signals, jealousy, and a final reconciliation.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Kevin, Alison, Nikki, Margo, Jesse, and Eric all have distinct comic voices, and the script gives them repeatable behavior patterns that make them easy to remember. The characters are strongest as types in a social comedy machine, with Kevin and Alison carrying the most emotional weight and the others functioning as lively orbiting forces.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: This is where the script has real juice: Kevin, Eric, Matt, Dave, Nikki, Alison, Amber, Margo, and Jesse all generate story when paired in different combinations. The bar scenes especially show a strong combinatorial engine, with every new pairing creating a fresh comic and romantic pressure point.

whats_special.headline: This is a lively, adult ensemble rom-com with a very saleable social engine: divorced men, sharp women, bars, golf, and a constant stream of romantic misfires. The script’s biggest asset is how playable it is — for actors, for directors who like banter and chemistry, and for buyers who want an R-rated relationship comedy with a clear audience and a contained footprint.

strengths.evidence: Kevin, Eric, Matt, Dave, Nikki, Alison, Amber, Margo, and Jesse all create new dynamics in the bar, golf, office, and wedding sequences.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives a producer a repeatable social-comedy machine where every pairing can generate a new scene, a new date, or a new humiliation. It will attract buyers looking for an adult ensemble piece with clear roles for comic actors who can spar, flirt, and pivot fast.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble is the engine.

strengths.evidence: Kevin repeatedly freezes, rubs his forehead, misreads women, gets trapped in awkward dates, and keeps trying to recover with a grin.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead role gives an actor a steady stream of public humiliation, romantic confusion, and self-aware charm, which is exactly the kind of part that can become a calling card. Mid-career comedic leads and actors looking to play lovable damage will see a lot of playable territory here.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Kevin is built for comic embarrassment.

strengths.evidence: Nikki is sharp and wounded, Alison is guarded and warm, Amber is sexually direct, Margo is outrageous, and Jesse is dry and physical.
strengths.what_it_means: Nikki, Alison, Amber, Margo, and Jesse each have a distinct comic temperature, which keeps the romantic field from feeling generic and gives casting real texture. That kind of female ensemble is attractive to buyers who want a rom-com that can support multiple strong actresses instead of one lead love interest.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The women are not interchangeable.

strengths.evidence: Internet dating, bar pickups, strip clubs, ex-spouses, and golf-course flirtation drive the story from start to finish.
strengths.what_it_means: This is a clean commercial lane for viewers who want sex, divorce, and midlife panic without the polish of a studio rom-com. It fits buyers who want an R-rated relationship comedy with a recognizable lifestyle world and easy trailer moments.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The adult dating lane is very clear.

strengths.evidence: Kevin’s dates with Alison are framed through golf, and the course becomes a place for flirting, scorekeeping, and status games.
strengths.what_it_means: Using golf as a dating and ego battleground gives the script a repeatable visual and behavioral hook that is easy to market and easy to stage. Sports-adjacent comedy buyers and actors who like playing vanity, competition, and flirtation in one scene will respond to it.
strengths.dimension_or_area: Golf becomes a comic relationship arena.

strengths.evidence: The story closes with a double wedding, a comic speech from Dave, and the ensemble pairing off in a celebratory finale.
strengths.what_it_means: The final wedding and double-couple payoff give the script a satisfying commercial finish that turns the dating mess into a crowd-pleasing resolution. That makes it easier to sell as a feel-good adult comedy rather than a one-note bachelor farce.
strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending pays off the romantic chaos.

classification.tone: Broad, bawdy, conversational, and sex-forward with a sentimental payoff

considerations.area: Kevin’s romantic target keeps shifting.
considerations.detail: The script’s biggest engine is also its most movable part: Kevin’s attention swings from Nikki to Margo to Alison to Amber, which keeps the comedy lively but can make the emotional center feel elastic. One direction would be to let Alison’s line of desire arrive a little earlier and more decisively so the audience feels the destination sooner while still enjoying the detours.

considerations.area: The middle leans on repeated dating reversals.
considerations.detail: The bar and date scenes are consistently funny, but several of them operate on the same comic beat: Kevin misreads the woman, gets corrected, and retreats. A next pass could vary the scene design by letting one or two encounters turn on a choice Kevin makes rather than only on a reveal from the woman.

considerations.area: The brand references are plentiful.
considerations.detail: Zoloft, Viagra, McDonald’s, Denny’s, Reece’s Cups, Dr. Pepper, Remy Martin, Belvedere, and Valtrex all appear in dialogue, so a clearance pass would be worthwhile before packaging. The good news is that the story itself does not depend on any one brand, so substitutions would protect the comedy without changing the engine.

considerations.area: The finale adds a larger event footprint.
considerations.detail: The mansion courtyard wedding gives the script a satisfying finish, but it also introduces the largest crowd and staging requirement in the piece. If a leaner production path were needed, the version of the ending where the same emotional payoff happens in a smaller venue would preserve the story while simplifying the event build.

considerations.area: The twin reveal is the signature turn.
considerations.detail: The Alison/Amber reveal is one of the script’s most marketable reversals, and it deserves to stay crystal clear in the build. A next pass could make sure the audience gets just enough visual and behavioral distinction early so the later reveal lands as a payoff rather than a reset.

The adult dating lane, Florida setting, and built-in bar/golf/office repeatability make it easy to market as a date-night comedy with clear trailer moments and modest production demands.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to stage adult romantic chaos with banter, bodies, and emotional bruises.
director_appeal.detail: The fun here is in orchestration: who sits where, who watches whom, and how each scene turns on a glance, a line, or a public embarrassment. It’s especially attractive to directors who can make contained locations feel alive and who know how to keep a large ensemble moving without losing the romantic spine.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Second-feature or established indie-comedy directors who already work well with ensemble dialogue and relationship friction. The material rewards someone who likes performance-forward scenes, clean blocking in bars and restaurants, and a confident handle on R-rated comic rhythm without needing spectacle.

lead_characters.hook: Kevin is a preppy, good-natured, chronically confused divorced guy who wants love, sex, and companionship in equal measure but keeps stepping on his own emotional rake. He’s vain enough to think he still has game, self-aware enough to know he doesn’t, and charming enough that people keep giving him another shot anyway.
lead_characters.name: Kevin Murphy
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of showcase territory Steve Carell had in The 40-Year-Old Virgin and later in Dan in Real Life — a lovable man-child whose embarrassment is the comedy and whose sincerity keeps the audience with him. Actors who can play wounded charm, physical awkwardness, and romantic sincerity in the same role will chase this because Kevin gets to be funny, needy, and unexpectedly tender.

lead_characters.hook: Nikki is Kevin’s ex-wife, and she has the sharp tongue, wounded pride, and sexual confidence of someone who has already survived the marriage and is not interested in pretending otherwise. She’s funny because she’s furious, and she’s compelling because the anger always sits on top of real hurt.
lead_characters.name: Nikki Murphy
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Laura Dern had in Marriage Story — a woman whose emotional intelligence and bite make every exchange feel alive, even when she’s cutting someone down. Mid-career dramatic actresses who want a part with comic venom, romantic history, and a final emotional turn will see real value here.

lead_characters.hook: Eric is Kevin’s cynical wingman, the guy who has already decided love is a scam but still can’t stop talking about it. He’s dry, suspicious, and funny in a way that makes him the script’s built-in reality check and one of its best banter engines.
lead_characters.name: Eric Johnson
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting-lead territory Ed O’Neill had in Married... with Children or the grounded comic ballast of a Philip Seymour Hoffman scene partner role — a man whose skepticism becomes the joke and the wisdom at the same time. Character actors with strong timing will want this because Eric gets to be the voice of experience without losing the laughs.

lead_characters.hook: Alison looks like the quiet office woman Kevin overlooks, then reveals herself as the emotional center of the story: smart, guarded, sensual, and carrying a history that makes trust feel expensive. She has the best kind of romantic-comedy contradiction — she seems reserved, but once she opens up, she has real heat and authority.
lead_characters.name: Alison
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space Sandra Bullock had in While You Were Sleeping and Jennifer Aniston had in The Break-Up — a woman whose warmth and self-protection are both part of the appeal. Actresses who can play intelligence, restraint, and a slow-burn romantic payoff will chase this because Alison gets the emotional handoff from guarded to fully chosen.

lead_characters.hook: Amber is Alison’s twin and the story’s wild-card sensual force: direct, teasing, and impossible to ignore. She’s the kind of character who can flip a scene from flirtation to humiliation in a single line, and she keeps the romantic triangle deliciously unstable.
lead_characters.name: Amber
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing territory Elizabeth Banks had in Zack and Miri Make a Porno — a sexually confident comic role that can be outrageous without losing intelligence. Actors who like playing bold, high-voltage women with a mischievous edge will be drawn to Amber because she gets the biggest comic entrances and reversals.

lead_characters.hook: Margo is the outrageous older woman who refuses to be invisible, and the script treats her as both comic chaos and a genuine force of appetite. She’s blunt, shameless, and weirdly self-possessed, which makes her more than a gag and gives her real scene power.
lead_characters.name: Margo
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Kathy Bates had in About Schmidt or June Squibb had in Nebraska — a late-life part that gets to be funny, sexual, and emotionally unfiltered. Veteran actresses who want a bold, memorable comic turn will chase Margo because she owns every room she enters.

lead_characters.hook: Jesse is the rough-edged, physically expressive woman who reads as a punchline at first and then reveals a dry, lonely intelligence underneath. She’s one of the script’s best examples of a character who can be funny, needy, and unexpectedly tender in the same breath.
lead_characters.name: Jesse
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Melissa McCarthy had in Bridesmaids before the industry knew exactly how to use her — a woman whose physicality and bluntness are the joke, but whose loneliness gives the part depth. Character actresses with fearless comic instincts will want Jesse because she can play broad and human at once.

lead_characters.hook: Matt is one of Kevin’s golf-and-bar friends, a blunt, horny, good-time guy who keeps the male banter moving. He’s less emotionally complicated than Kevin or Eric, which makes him useful as comic pressure and social contrast.
lead_characters.name: Matt
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a comic actor the easy confidence of a Fred Willard-style scene partner — a guy who can land a line and keep the ensemble moving. Supporting comic players who like fast banter and group chemistry will be interested because Matt is a reliable laugh engine.

lead_characters.hook: Dave is the therapist in the group, but he’s also the most sexually open and socially surprising of the men, which makes him the script’s slyest wildcard. He can sound like the voice of reason one minute and the most unfiltered guy in the room the next.
lead_characters.name: Dave
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play against expectation the way Paul Rudd did in This Is 40 — a seemingly grounded guy who keeps revealing stranger, funnier edges. Character actors who like playing calm authority with a dirty comic undercurrent will want Dave.

lead_characters.hook: Leah is the polished, predatory date who looks like fantasy and behaves like a transaction, which makes her a sharp comic trap for Kevin. She’s there to expose his delusion, and she does it with a cool, cutting confidence.
lead_characters.name: Leah
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene role that gives an actress a fast, memorable turn in the vein of the date-night reversals in Knocked Up or Swingers. Actors who like playing the woman who controls the room for one scene will be drawn to Leah because she lands a clean comic sting.
